A STROOP EFFECT WITHOUT A HUMAN

2026-11-14 · Metacheck 0.4.4.1

3to fix2to check0to decide by hand1fine9not applicable

To fix (3)

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 59 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 16 of 596 data columns (3%) are documented in a codebook; 580 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (59 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 3% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents sample, ex_ID, ID while the data has sample, ID, orig_ID. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 6 codebook/README/label sources and 596 data columns across 18 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (59 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 3% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents sample, ex_ID, ID while the data has sample, ID, orig_ID. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

ex_ID Pseudonym of Gorilla’s Participant Public ID (X0001 to X0153) CODEBOOK.md
ID Pseudonym of Gorilla’s Participant Private ID (1001 to 1153); the respondent key used in all analyses CODEBOOK.md
trial_number Position of the trial among the 288 main trials (1 to 288) CODEBOOK.md
display Gorilla display name; always Trials CODEBOOK.md
congruency congruent (word matches ink color), neutral (word is XXXX) or incongruent (word differs from ink color) CODEBOOK.md
stimulus Stimulus as stored in the Gorilla spreadsheet: HTML with the ink color as a hex code and the word in bold, e.g. <span style="color:#0000FF;"><strong>RED</strong></span> is RED in blue ink (#FF0000 red, #008000 green, #0000FF blue, #FFFF00 yellow) CODEBOOK.md
response Key response as recorded by Gorilla: red, green, blue, yellow (keys R, G, B, Y), or missed (no response within 2,000 ms) CODEBOOK.md
rt Response time. For missed trials, Gorilla’s logged time of the timeout event; it is not a response time and is never analyzed CODEBOOK.md
correct 1 if the response matched the ink color; misses are coded 0 CODEBOOK.md
missed TRUE if no response was given within 2,000 ms CODEBOOK.md
rt_valid TRUE for correct, non-missed trials; only these enter response time measures CODEBOOK.md
sample, ID, ex_ID As in trials_all.csv CODEBOOK.md
n_trials Number of main trials; always 288 CODEBOOK.md
accuracy Task accuracy over all 288 trials (misses count as incorrect) CODEBOOK.md
mean_rt Mean correct response time over all conditions CODEBOOK.md
n_missed Number of missed trials CODEBOOK.md
prop_miss n_missed / 288 CODEBOOK.md
n_keys Number of different response keys used (misses not counted) CODEBOOK.md
accuracy_congruent, accuracy_neutral, accuracy_incongruent Task accuracy within each condition (96 trials each) CODEBOOK.md
mean_rt_congruent, mean_rt_neutral, mean_rt_incongruent Mean correct response time within each condition; empty if the condition has no correct response CODEBOOK.md
congruency_effect mean_rt_incongruent − mean_rt_congruent; used in quality check 4 and Figure 2b CODEBOOK.md
facilitation mean_rt_neutral − mean_rt_congruent; classifier feature CODEBOOK.md
interference mean_rt_incongruent − mean_rt_neutral; classifier feature CODEBOOK.md
sample, ID, ex_ID, accuracy, mean_rt, n_missed, prop_miss, n_keys, congruency_effect As in respondent_summary.csv CODEBOOK.md
rt_cong, rt_incong Same as mean_rt_congruent and mean_rt_incongruent CODEBOOK.md
rt_sample_mean, rt_sample_sd Mean and SD of mean_rt within the respondent’s own sample CODEBOOK.md
rt_z (mean_rt − rt_sample_mean) / rt_sample_sd CODEBOOK.md
flag_accuracy Check 1: accuracy < .80 CODEBOOK.md
flag_fast_rt Check 2: mean_rt < 300 ms CODEBOOK.md
flag_rt_3sd Check 3:   CODEBOOK.md
flag_no_congruency Check 4: rt_incong ≤ rt_cong, or either is empty CODEBOOK.md
flag_missed Check 5: prop_miss > .10 CODEBOOK.md
flag_invariant Check 6: n_keys < 4 CODEBOOK.md
flag_any TRUE if any of the six flags is TRUE CODEBOOK.md
respondents_in_export Respondents in the raw export CODEBOOK.md
with_experimental_trials Respondents with at least one main-trial response CODEBOOK.md
analyzed Respondents analyzed (51 per sample) CODEBOOK.md
not_analyzed_no_trials Respondents without main-trial responses CODEBOOK.md
not_analyzed_draw Online respondents not selected in the random draw of 51 of 54 CODEBOOK.md
sample Always AGEA CODEBOOK.md
ID AGEA_001 to AGEA_051; the prefix keeps these IDs apart from the integer IDs of the other samples CODEBOOK.md
orig_ID Order-preserving pseudonym of Gorilla’s Participant Private ID (1 to 51); ID is built from it CODEBOOK.md
ex_ID Pseudonym of Gorilla’s Participant Public ID; one value (AGEAX001) because all sessions ran under one public ID CODEBOOK.md
source_file Raw file the row came from (raw_agea.csv) CODEBOOK.md
trial_number, display, congruency, response, rt, correct, missed, rt_valid As in trials_all.csv CODEBOOK.md
stimulus Gorilla stimulus ID in the form WORD_inkcolor, e.g. GREEN_blue is GREEN in blue ink; XXXX_red is a neutral trial in red ink CODEBOOK.md
Participant Public ID Respondent code (pseudonymized, see above) README.md
Participant Private ID Gorilla’s internal respondent number README.md
Task Name Task; only the Stroop task is in these files README.md
Display Screen type; Trials = main trials, Practice = practice trials (others are instructions and breaks) README.md
Trial Number Trial position within the display README.md
Response Type Kind of row; only response rows (the key press or timeout) are analyzed README.md
Response red, green, blue, yellow, or missed (no response within 2,000 ms) README.md
Reaction Time Response time in ms from stimulus onset README.md
Correct 1 if the response matched the ink color (a miss is rescored as incorrect in the analysis) README.md
Spreadsheet: Congruency congruent, neutral or incongruent README.md
Spreadsheet: Stimulus_text Stimulus as HTML (word and ink color); used for the lab, online and AEA files README.md
Spreadsheet: Stimulus_ID Stimulus as WORD_inkcolor; used for the AGEA file README.md

To fix Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 46 files: 18 data, 16 code, 10 documentation, 2 materials.
  • We found 18 tabular data files and extracted 596 columns from 18 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 1 study group (ex1), plus 4 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata). We ran automated data-quality checks on 596 columns; 198 columns have at least one potential issue (154 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 100 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 8 columns with numeric values stored as text).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 596 columns across 18 data files.

Issues Identified

198 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 18 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • 01_data_processing.Rmd reads raw_lab.csv.
  • 02_quality_and_visual.Rmd reads trials_all.csv.
  • 04_agea_data_processing.Rmd reads raw_agea.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A script uses a location that exists only on your computer.

  • 00_anonymize_raw.py reads /raw_original/lab_data_exp_267618-v3_tasks.csv.

No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit.

  1. Add the file to the deposit.
  2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here(“data”, “survey.csv”) does this for you.
  3. Remove any setwd() lines.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • 03_classification.ipynb: display

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

One approach to identifying agent-generated data is to apply exclusion criteria developed for human participants.

Online participants were recruited through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com), completed the task remotely on their own devices, and received £3 as compensation.

All lab and online participants gave informed consent before beginning the task, took part voluntarily, and could stop at any time.

Development of the AEA took place in January 2026, before human data collection, and no data from our participants were provided to the system.

Participants were instructed to identify the ink color and to ignore the semantic content of the word.

Each cubicle contained a desktop computer with a monitor, a keyboard, and a mouse; participants were seated approximately 60 cm from the screen.

Participants read an information letter and provided informed consent.

Online participants completed an identical copy of the experiment remotely on their own devices, with no supervision and no control over viewing conditions.

Most existing bot-detection and authenticity checks are built into survey platforms or applied before participants enter a study (CloudResearch, n.d.; Prolific, 2026).

To our knowledge, as of November 2026, only one sample provider offers checks that run during a study (Prolific, 2026).

To illustrate this, in October 2026 the first author advertised a study on Prolific that was set up only for this test.

4 The AGEA completed the study undetected, without any warning or flag from Prolific.

No other participants took part, and the reward was paid only to that account.

Sampling frame Method: Samples Lab: university students; online: Prolific, 51 of 54 drawn; AEA: 51 respondents 3c.

Ethics approval statement:

The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University (reference 26-0757).

Ethics: The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University (reference 26-0757).

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
