How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Researchers have long assumed that online behavioral experiments are completed by humans, an assumption AI agents can now violate. We asked whether agent and human data can be distinguished. We compared Stroop data from 51 respondents each: humans verified in person, an artificial experiment agent, and an online sample. All agent-generated respondents showed the congruency effect and passed six quality checks. A one-class support vector machine (SVM) trained only on human data achieved a median accuracy of 63%. A supervised SVM trained on human and agent data achieved 94%. At an assumed 5% contamination rate, most of its flags would be false alarms. The supervised SVM did not generalize to an agent it was not trained on. Neither plausible task performance nor the tested SVMs reliably distinguished human from agent data. These findings suggest that human participation should be safeguarded through study design rather than through screening afterward.

A "Human-Like" Stroop Effect No Longer Implies a Human Participant

Over the past decade, online recruitment platforms have become increasingly important for social science research, allowing researchers to recruit large and diverse samples quickly (Stewart et al., 2017). More recently, advances in artificial agents based on large language models (LLMs) have raised concerns about the integrity of online research. Westwood (2025) showed that LLM-based synthetic respondents can pass as human participants in online surveys, which may pose an existential threat to online survey research. Agents can also complete online behavioral experiments, in some cases with response times and accuracies close to those of humans (Huskey et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026). These studies showed that AI agents can match human data on broad measures, but did not test whether more detailed features could distinguish agent data (data from sessions in which an AI agent completes the experiment) from human data. Here, we ask whether human and agent data collected in identical versions of a behavioral experiment can be reliably distinguished from the behavioral data alone.

Whether AI agents already threaten online behavioral experiments is contested.

Some researchers have warned that response time studies may already contain agent-generated data (Van der Stigchel et al., 2026); others have argued that task-specific agents are not yet economical to build and that unusual response times are not evidence of bots (Brand et al., 2026; Chetverikov, 2026). Still others have countered that once the behavioral markers that distinguish agents from humans are documented, agents can be built to avoid them, so that the markers lose their value for detection (Westwood & Frederick, 2026). For online surveys, the evidence is more direct: on several platforms, online respondents failed validated AI-detection tests far more often than verified in-person participants, and an agent built with full knowledge of the tests went undetected, although it was slower and costlier to run than a human participant (Zhang et al., 2026).

Differences between humans and AI systems in how they process information have been proposed both as architectural limitations of LLMs and as a basis for detecting AI agents. For example, accuracy losses of LLMs on incongruent Stroop items were interpreted as a lack of executive control (Patel et al., 2026). Cognitive traps based on reported limitations of vision-language models were presented as an effective way to detect agents in online surveys (Affonso, 2026a). These differences need not be inherent : Patel et al. (2026) also noted that a reasoning model solved the task by writing and executing code, and a public repository of cognitive-trap results suggests that recent models increasingly pass these traps (Affonso, 2026b).

Agentic AI systems can overcome limitations of the LLMs they are built on. They add tools, retrieval, and memory to the LLM and let it direct its own tool use in a loop based on feedback from the environment (Anthropic, 2024). Current commercial agents (e.g., Anthropic, n.d. ; Google, 2025) complete everyday tasks on websites, such as booking a ticket, and can also complete online behavioral experiments. In a Stroop task, for example, an agent could read the ink color with code instead of resolving the conflict between word and color. Therefore, poor performance of an LLM in one configuration (e.g., without code execution) neither indicates an inherent limitation nor rules out a threat to online research.

One approach to identifying agent-generated data is to apply exclusion criteria developed for human participants. In surveys, exclusion criteria are commonly based on attention checks and completion times (Meade & Craig, 2012; Oppenheimer et al., 2009); in response time tasks, on accuracy (e.g., Khng & Lee, 2014; La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025).

Methods have also been developed to catch the scripted bots of the pre-LLM era, often by looking for random responding (Dupuis et al., 2019; Griffin et al., 2022). LLM-based agents differ from both, because they complete the task through the same interface as human participants and can produce human-like mean response times and accuracies (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026). However, whether existing checks or detection methods can identify agent-generated data in behavioral experiments has not been tested.

We tested the possibility of identifying agent-generated data with the color-word Stroop task (Stroop, 1935). The Stroop task is a useful test case because its congruency effect, slower responses when the word and the ink color conflict, is one of the most reliable findings in experimental psychology (MacLeod, 1991; Van Maanen et al., 2009). It is also present in most individual participants (Haaf & Rouder, 2019), so its absence may indicate that the participant did not perform the task as intended, and it has been used as an exclusion criterion (e.g., La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025).

We compared three samples of 51 respondents each (a respondent being one lab or online participant, or one task completion by the artificial experiment agent [AEA]) from the same Stroop task: from humans tested in the lab and verified in person, from the prompt-built AEA, and from an online platform. We addressed three research questions.

First, would conventional quality checks and visual inspection identify agent-generated data? Second, how well could machine-learning classifiers distinguish agent from human data when trained on verified human data alone or on labeled data from both humans and agents? Third, how should the classifiers' output be interpreted for the online data, where it is uncertainfoot_0 whether they came from humans?

Study Disclosures

Preregistration: No aspects of this study were preregistered. Materials: The prompts used to develop the AEA and the resulting agent application will be made available to reviewers. To prevent malicious use, these materials will not be shared publicly. Researchers may request access from the authors, subject to Utrecht University's nondisclosure agreement. Data and analysis scripts: All data and scripts required to reproduce the reported analyses, tables, and figures are archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24129387) and available in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/tlhzdgr/AEA), together with a README that explains how to reproduce the analyses and lists the required software and package versions.

Method Samples

We analyzed data from three samples of 51 respondents each: a lab sample of human participants verified in person, an AEA sample generated by the agent described in the next subsection, and an online sample of participants tested remotely. Sample size was determined by the feasibility of lab recruitment, and the AEA and online samples were matched to the lab sample in size only. Because no prior estimate of effect size was available for the classification analyses, no power analysis was conducted.

The lab sample comprised 51 Utrecht University students recruited through the university's recruitment platform. Eligibility criteria were age (18 years or older), normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and no color blindness. Participants received 0.5 participation credits. A researcher, who was present throughout each session (see the Procedure section), verified that the data came from human participants. Online participants were recruited through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com), completed the task remotely on their own devices, and received £3 as compensation. Fifty-four respondents completed the task, and none were excluded beforehand. To match the lab sample size and allow direct comparison between the samples, 51 of these 54 respondents were selected at random, before any quality check was applied. All lab and online participants gave informed consent before beginning the task, took part voluntarily, and could stop at any time. All reported being fluent in English. The study was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University (reference 26-0757). No procedures to prevent or screen out automated or AI-generated responses were used during data collection, because neither the recruitment platform nor the experiment-hosting platform offered such checks for this experiment; detecting such responses afterward was the subject of this study.

Artificial Experiment Agent

The AEA was developed using Google Antigravity (Google, 2025), an agentic AI development platform, as an extension of the work described in Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al. (2026). Development of the AEA took place in January 2026, before human data collection, and no data from our participants were provided to the system.

Throughout the interaction with the development platform, the first author adopted a layperson persona, beginning with one detailed prompt and continuing with conversational follow-up prompts, reflecting how a lay user might naturally interact with a large language model. The initial prompt gave only the link to the experiment and did not name the task, its conditions, or its expected effects. It asked the agent to identify the task from the on-screen instructions and to model human response times and accuracy using the available literature on the task. The AEA was built from natural-language prompts only, and no code was written or edited by the authors. To reduce the risk of malicious use, further implementation details are withheld from the public description; access arrangements for reviewers and researchers are described in the Research Transparency Statement.

Task and Design

The color-word Stroop task (Stroop, 1935) was implemented in Gorilla Experiment Builder (https://www.gorilla.sc). Stimuli were the words RED, GREEN, BLUE, and YELLOW and a neutral stimulus XXXX, each presented in one of four ink colors (red, green, blue, or yellow), at a font size of 60 px centered on a white screen. The task included congruent, incongruent, and neutral trials, in which the word respectively matched the ink color, differed from it, or was XXXX (see Figure 1). Participants were instructed to identify the ink color and to ignore the semantic content of the word. They responded by pressing the standard keyboard keys R, G, B, or Y.

A practice block of 12 trials (four congruent, four incongruent, and four neutral trials) was presented in the same fixed order for all participants. During practice, feedback followed each response: a green tick for a correct response and a red cross for an incorrect one, each displayed for 400 ms. The main experiment consisted of 288 trials, 96 per condition, presented in a different random order for each participant. The trials were divided into three blocks of 96 separated by two self-paced breaks (after trials 96 and 192), which participants ended by pressing the space bar. The composition of the blocks was not constrained.

Each trial began with a fixation cross presented for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus, which remained on screen until a response was given or for at most 2,000 ms. If no response was given within 2,000 ms, the message "Too slow!" was shown for 400 ms and the trial was coded as a miss. Every trial ended with a 500 ms blank screen before the next trial began. The structure of the task and a single trial are shown in Figure 1. The task took approximately 10 minutes to complete. a b Congruent Incongruent Neutral Fixation 500 ms Stimulus ≤ 2,000 ms Blank 500 ms Next trial begins > 2,000 ms 400 ms RED RED XXXX + RED Too slow! Note. Panel a shows example stimuli for the three conditions; panel b shows one trial.

Procedure

All data were collected between April and May 2026, except the AGEA data (see the Supplemental Material). Lab sessions took place in individual cubicles at Utrecht University. Each cubicle contained a desktop computer with a monitor, a keyboard, and a mouse; participants were seated approximately 60 cm from the screen. Room lighting was dimmed and monitor brightness was held constant across sessions to standardize color perception. The task ran in a web browser, so the lab computers were connected to the internet. Participants read an information letter and provided informed consent. At least one student researcher was present throughout each session.

Online participants completed an identical copy of the experiment remotely on their own devices, with no supervision and no control over viewing conditions.

The AEA completed the task 51 times, one session at a time, on another identical copy of the experiment. All sessions ran on a personal computer with Windows 11 Enterprise.

Data Processing and Analysis

Data were processed in R 4.5.2 (R Core Team, 2025). Each trial of the main experiment was coded as a correct response, an incorrect response (i.e., a key press not matching the ink color), or a miss (i.e., no response before the 2,000 ms deadline). For all respondents, all 288 main trials were retained, and practice trials were not analyzed. Task accuracy per respondent was computed as the proportion of correct responses across all trials, with misses counted as incorrect. Response time measures in the quality checks and the congruency effects were based on correct responses only. No response time trimming was applied, and no data were excluded at this stage.

We analyzed the data in three steps: (a) we applied conventional quality checks to all data, (b) we tested whether AEA data could be detected with support vector machines, and (c) we applied these detectors to the online sample.

Conventional Quality Checks

We applied six quality-check criteria to all respondents in all three samples. Criteria of this kind are commonly used to exclude data in response time studies (Khng & Lee, 2014; La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025). A respondent was flagged if any of the following was true (a flagged respondent is one that a researcher would usually exclude): (1) task accuracy below .80, (2) mean correct response time below 300 ms, (3) mean correct response time more than 3 standard deviations above or below the mean of its sample, (4) no congruency effect, that is, mean correct response time on incongruent trials no longer than on congruent trials (MacLeod, 1991), (5) more than 10% of trials missed, or (6) fewer than four different response keys used. The thresholds were set by the authors, based on criteria used in prior work (Khng & Lee, 2014; La Pietra & Ruzzoli, 2025). An accuracy below .80 indicates frequent errors in a task with four response options in which most responses should be correct.

A mean correct response time below 300 ms is too fast to be realistic for identifying an ink color and pressing the matching key. A deviation of more than 3 standard deviations from the sample mean is a common criterion for outliers (Leys et al., 2018). The congruency effect is one of the most reliable findings in experimental psychology (MacLeod, 1991), so its absence suggests that the task was not performed as instructed. More than 10% missed trials indicates a lack of attention, given the 2,000 ms response deadline, and using fewer than four response keys means that at least one ink color was never reported. The same thresholds were used for all three samples. For criterion 3, the mean and standard deviation of the respondents' mean correct response times were computed separately for each sample. No data were removed because of a quality-check flag.

We also inspected the data visually, as a researcher might do when screening experimental data. Data from ten respondents, five lab and five AEA, were drawn at random and shuffled. For each respondent, we plotted the distribution of correct response times, the accuracy per condition, and the congruency effect.

Detection With Support Vector Machines

We then tested how well AEA data could be detected from the data alone, in two situations. In the first, we mimicked a researcher who has only verified human data and tries to detect respondents that differ from them, which is an anomaly detection problem.

For this problem, we applied a one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001). In the second, we mimicked a researcher who has also built an agent, as we did with the AEA, and can use its data to train a classifier that tells human and agent data apart. Here we used a supervised binary SVM to differentiate the classes (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995). Both classification analyses were run in Python 3.12 with scikit-learn 1.7 (Pedregosa et al., 2011). We followed the REFORMS checklist for machine-learning-based science (Kapoor et al., 2024); the completed checklist is given in Table S6 of the Supplemental Material. To show which features separated the lab and AEA samples on their own, we also computed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for each feature across all 51 lab and 51 AEA respondents, without a classifier. We report the AUC in whichever direction separated the samples better.

Models. The one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001) encodes "normal" data by learning a boundary that encloses most of the training data, here the human lab data only.

New respondents that fall outside this boundary are treated as anomalies. We counted an anomaly as a flag for possible AEA data. We used a radial basis function kernel. The parameter ν is a model setting that, in theory, sets an upper limit on the share of training respondents that fall outside the boundary. In practice, the share of training respondents flagged can be higher, because respondents that lie on the boundary can also be flagged.

Both ν and the kernel can strongly affect how well a one-class SVM performs, and there are no definite rules for choosing the kernel (Hejazi & Singh, 2013). Without labeled AEA data, which a one-class detector does not use, there is also no clear way to select these settings from the data. We therefore fixed ν = .08 in advance and used scikit-learn's default kernel width, without tuning either setting. To test whether this choice affected the results, we repeated the analysis with 1,000 splits for values of ν from .01 to .50. Median classifier accuracy varied only between .62 and .63 (Table S1 in the Supplemental Material), so our conclusions do not depend on ν within this range. The supervised binary SVM was trained on labeled lab and AEA data to separate the two. It used a radial basis function kernel with scikit-learn's default regularization (C = 1) and kernel width. For both SVMs, we call a respondent classified as AEA flagged; unlike a quality-check flag, this is a classification, not a judgment of data quality.

Classifier Evaluation.

To determine classifier performance, we used cross-validation: we split each of the lab and AEA samples at random into a training set and a test set and then combined them, so that every training set and every test set contained equal numbers of lab and AEA respondents. We repeated this 5,000 times, as suggested for small samples (Monte Carlo cross-validation; Shan, 2022). In each split, 25 lab and 25 AEA respondents were used for training, and the other 26 lab and 26 AEA respondents for testing. The one-class SVM was trained on the 25 lab respondents in the training set only, and the supervised binary SVM on all 50. The features were standardized with the means and standard deviations of each SVM's own training data (lab only for the one-class SVM), and the same values were applied to the test data. Both SVMs were tested on the same 52 test respondents. For each split, we computed three measures.

Classifier sensitivity is the share of AEA test respondents that were flagged: sensitivity = true positives true positives + false negatives where true positives are AEA respondents that were flagged and false negatives are AEA respondents that were not flagged. Specificity is the share of lab test respondents that were not flagged: specificity = true negatives true negatives + false positives where true negatives are lab respondents that were not flagged and false positives are lab respondents that were flagged. Classifier accuracy is the share of all test respondents classified correctly: accuracy = true positives + true negatives all test respondents

We report the median and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across splits. The percentiles show how much classifier performance varied between splits; they are not confidence intervals. Means were almost the same as medians. As a robustness check with more training data, we also ran repeated 10-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation once on all 102 respondents. These gave similar results for the supervised binary SVM and a somewhat higher classifier accuracy for the one-class SVM (.67), mainly because fewer lab respondents were flagged (Table S2 in the Supplemental Material). To test whether the supervised binary SVM generalized beyond the agent it was trained on, we collected data from 51 respondents generated by a second agent, the artificial general experiment agent (AGEA).

The AGEA was developed by the first author in a separate project to complete behavioral experiments in general rather than the Stroop task alone (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026), and it completed the same task. These data served only as an additional test of the supervised binary SVM; the analysis is reported in the Supplemental Material (Table S5).

Application to the Online Sample

The splits above estimate how well the SVMs perform, but each split used only half of the data for training. To show how a researcher would apply the method in practice, we refit both SVMs once on all available data: the one-class SVM on all 51 lab respondents and the supervised binary SVM on all 102 lab and AEA respondents, with the features standardized using each SVM's own training data. We then applied both SVMs to the online sample as an illustration. The online data were not used for training or evaluation because their composition is unknown. One online respondent had no correct response on incongruent trials, so its interference could not be computed; the SVMs were therefore applied to the other 50 online respondents. We report the number and proportion of flagged online respondents with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals (Brown et al., 2001).

Positive Predictive Value.

A flag is only useful if a flagged respondent is likely to be an agent. This probability, the positive predictive value (PPV), depends on the sensitivity and specificity of a detector and on the proportion π of agent respondents in the sample:

In the cross-validation, classifier performance was determined using test sets in which half of the test respondents were AEA respondents, which is far more than we would expect in a real sample. Because the composition of the online sample was unknown, we computed the PPV for three assumed contamination rates (5%, 10%, and 20%), using the unrounded median sensitivity and specificity from Table 2. These PPV calculations assume that the SVMs would make the same proportion of errors on online data as on the lab and AEA test data, which we could not check without verified online data. The PPVs in Table 4 use the median sensitivity and specificity; their variation across splits is given in the table note.

In the Supplemental Material, we also tested whether a more cautious supervised binary SVM, with stricter thresholds or with class weights matching each assumed contamination rate, would make its flags more trustworthy when agents are rare (Table S4).

Results

Conventional Quality Checks

We first asked whether the checks that researchers routinely use would exclude AEA data: common exclusion criteria and visual inspection.

None of the 51 lab respondents and none of the 51 AEA respondents was flagged by any of the six quality-check criteria (Table 1). The AEA respondents also stayed well clear of every threshold: their lowest task accuracy was .92, their fastest mean correct response time was 584 ms, no AEA respondent had more than 3 misses in 288 trials, and every AEA respondent showed a congruency effect of at least 113 ms. Conventional screening would therefore have excluded no AEA respondents. From the online sample, a single respondent was flagged: its task accuracy was .65, and it had no correct response on incongruent trials, so its congruency effect could not be computed. Because the online data were collected without in-person verification, we cannot determine whether this respondent was a human or an agent.

Visual Inspection

Exclusion criteria check each threshold separately, but researchers also look at the data as a whole. Figure 2 shows the ten respondents: panel a shows the distribution of correct response times and the accuracy per condition (the proportion of correct responses among the 96 trials of each condition), and panel b shows the congruency effect. Readers can test themselves by trying to identify the AEA respondents before checking the answer in the footnote.

Both groups showed right-skewed response time distributions, high accuracy, and a positive congruency effect, and this held for all 51 lab and all 51 AEA respondents. None of the AEA respondents showed a pattern that would have typically led to exclusion based on visual inspection, although the AEA respondents had more skewed distributions and larger congruency effects on average, mainly because of larger facilitation (Table S3 in the

Visual Inspection: Can You Distinguish Data From the Artificial Experiment Agent (AEA)

From Human Data?

Detection With Support Vector Machines

We next asked whether AEA data can be detected from the data alone. We used two SVMs for two situations a researcher might face: a one-class SVM trained only on verified human data, and a supervised binary SVM trained on labeled human and agent data. Both used eight input features and were tested on held-out data across 5,000 random splits.

Performance on Lab and AEA Data

Table 2 and Figure 3 summarize the performance of both SVMs on the test respondents across the 5,000 splits. With only verified human data, the one-class SVM performed poorly (median classifier accuracy = .63). It flagged nearly all AEA test respondents (sensitivity = .88) but also about three in five lab test respondents (specificity = .38); the middle 95% of its accuracies across splits lay between .50 and .75, so in some splits it performed no better than chance. With labeled AEA data, the supervised binary SVM reached a median classifier accuracy of .94 (mean = .93): it flagged nearly all AEA test respondents (sensitivity = .96) and wrongly flagged about one in eight lab test respondents (specificity = .88). Detection was therefore much better when labeled AEA data were available, but some lab respondents were still flagged. On their own, the best single features were facilitation (AUC = .91), response time skewness (.90), and response time autocorrelation (.84), whereas task accuracy separated the samples poorly (.60; Table S3 in the Supplemental Material).

Generalization to a Second Agent

A supervised SVM is useful only if it generalizes, that is, if it also correctly classifies respondents from an agent that it was not trained on. We therefore tested the performance of the supervised binary SVM on data from a second agent, the AGEA, which was designed to complete behavioral experiments in general (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026). The supervised SVM did not generalize at its default decision threshold: trained on AEA data, it flagged 19% of the AGEA respondents, and its balanced accuracy dropped from .94 to .54. Conversely, when trained on the AGEA data, a supervised SVM flagged 35% of the AEA respondents, with its balanced accuracy dropping from .96 to .67 (Table S5 in the Supplemental Material). An SVM trained on data from one agent therefore did not detect respondents of an agent it had not been trained on.

Application to the Online Sample

Finally, we asked how flags from both SVMs should be interpreted in an online study, where the share of agents or simpler bots is unknown. We refit both SVMs on all lab and AEA data and applied them to the online sample of 50 classifiable respondents. Recall that all 50 classifiable online respondents had passed the quality checks; the one respondent that failed them could not be classified. Because the composition of this online sample is unknown, we have no ground truth to interpret the flags; flagged online respondents therefore did not necessarily come from agents. The two SVMs differed in how many of the online respondents they flagged (Table 3). The one-class SVM flagged 22 respondents (.44). If all 50 online respondents were human, the SVM's false-alarm rate for lab data would produce about 21 false alarms when it was trained on 50 lab respondents (leave-one-out, .41) and about 31 when it was trained on 25 (main splits, .62). The 22 flags are within this range, so they cannot separate agents from humans. Because the one-class SVM flags anomalies compared with the lab data, its flags may also reflect differences between remote and lab testing, such as devices and testing environments.

The supervised binary SVM flagged five online respondents (.10). With its false-alarm rate for lab data (.10 in leave-one-out, .12 in the main splits), about five to six false alarms would be expected if all 50 online respondents were human, so these five flags do not by themselves indicate agent participation. Two online respondents were flagged by both SVMs. We again emphasize that we could not verify whether the online respondents were human and that these flags should therefore not be read as evidence of agent contamination in this sample. (Brown et al., 2001). SVM = support vector machine; AEA = artificial experiment agent; CI = confidence interval.

Positive Predictive Value

Table 4 shows the PPV at the three assumed contamination rates. The one-class SVM's PPV was only slightly higher than the assumed contamination rate in each scenario (.07, .14, and .26 at 5%, 10%, and 20%), so even at 20% contamination about three in four of its flags would be false alarms. The supervised SVM did better, but its PPV was still low when agents were rare. At 5% contamination, it was .30: about three in ten flagged respondents would truly be agents, and seven in ten would be false alarms. Even at 20% contamination, about one in three flags would be a false alarm. More cautious settings, that is, stricter thresholds (higher cut-offs, so the SVM needs more evidence before flagging a respondent) or class weights matching a low contamination rate, reduced false alarms, on average, only by missing more AEA respondents (Table S4 in the Supplemental Material).

High accuracy in a balanced evaluation therefore does not justify treating flagged respondents as agents. Note. The three rates are illustrative scenarios, not estimates for the online sample. Across the 5,000 splits, the 2.5th percentile of the PPV was .05, .10, and .20 for the one-class SVM and .21, .36, and .56 for the supervised SVM. SVM = support vector machine; AEA = artificial experiment agent.

Discussion

Several studies have shown that AI agents can complete online surveys (Westwood, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) and online behavioral experiments, in some cases with human-like response times and accuracies (Huskey et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026). Can AEA respondents still be detected from their data alone? Our results show that the AEA respondents passed all conventional quality checks and looked plausible on visual inspection next to lab respondents. A one-class SVM trained only on lab data performed poorly at detecting AEA respondents, and a supervised binary SVM trained on labeled AEA and lab data performed well but still flagged some lab respondents.

In practice, having only verified human data is the more realistic situation, because labeled agent data are rarely available for online samples. Our one-class SVM used only such data but incorrectly flagged about three in five of the lab test respondents. Several features separated the lab and AEA samples on average, but their distributions overlapped, so some AEA respondents closely resembled lab respondents (Table S3). For the one-class SVM, the limit therefore lies in this overlap, not only in the choice of classifier.

The supervised SVM reached high classifier accuracy in a balanced evaluation, but its practical value depends on more than accuracy. When agents are rare in a sample, even a small false-alarm rate produces many false alarms: at an assumed contamination rate of 5%, most respondents flagged as agents would actually be human, if the observed error rates held. More cautious settings did not solve this problem: on average, they reduced false alarms only by missing more AEA respondents.

The online sample illustrates these false alarms: both SVMs flagged about as many respondents as their false-alarm rates would predict if all respondents were human. Neither set of flags therefore estimates contamination, and respondents that were not flagged cannot be certified as human. Automatically excluding flagged respondents could remove much valid data and introduce bias if errors affected some groups of participants more than others.

Two further constraints limit supervised detection in practice. First, researchers cannot be expected to build an agent, collect data with it, and train a classifier before every online study. Second, although building such an agent becomes easier as models improve (see Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026), nothing guarantees that a researcher's agent resembles the agents used by fraudulent participants. Different prompts, tools, or response strategies could remove the features on which the separation depended. Our second agent showed that this can happen: an SVM trained on one agent missed most respondents of the other (Table S5).

Our findings have practical implications for how online behavioral data are collected, evaluated, and reported. Researchers should no longer treat valid task performance or conventional exclusion criteria as sufficient evidence of human participation. Participant verification should become part of study design, because detection and data cleaning after collection may not be enough. Journals and reviewers can support this by asking authors to report how human participation was verified.

Online sample providers and experiment-hosting platforms carry great responsibility, because they control infrastructure that individual researchers cannot reproduce. Gordon et al. (2026) argued that reported agent capabilities do not show actual contamination and that some platforms already screen respondents at enrollment and monitor them over time.

These claims require further support. Most existing bot-detection and authenticity checks are built into survey platforms or applied before participants enter a study (CloudResearch, n.d.; Prolific, 2026). To our knowledge, as of November 2026, only one sample provider offers checks that run during a study (Prolific, 2026). These checks work on three platforms. Only one of them, Pavlovia, is designed to host behavioral experiments. 3 Protection during the behavioral experiment itself therefore remains largely a gap.

To illustrate this, in October 2026 the first author advertised a study on Prolific that was set up only for this test. The AGEA (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026) then took part in this study through another researcher's participant account. 4 The AGEA completed the study undetected, without any warning or flag from Prolific. This single test does not show how common agent participation is, but it shows that the capability can be used in practice.

3 These checks were not yet available on Pavlovia (pavlovia.org) when we collected our data, and they are still not available on Gorilla (gorilla.sc), which hosted our Stroop task. 4 The account holder consented to the use of the account. No other participants took part, and the reward was paid only to that account.

Platforms should therefore develop participant-verification and bot-detection measures that work across experiment-hosting environments. Independent researchers should be able to test these measures, because platforms may not disclose how they work.

These tests need to be repeated with each new generation of models, because safeguards built on current model limitations may lose their effectiveness.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, we examined one task, one hosting platform, and two agents, both developed by the first author, so we cannot say whether vulnerability or detectability depends on features of the task, although studies with other tasks suggest that the concern is broader (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026; Özüdoğru, Van der Stigchel, et al., 2026). Using the Stroop task may also have made human-like data easier to produce. It is among the most studied paradigms in psychology, so its typical results have likely entered the training data of current models. Yet less familiar tasks are not necessarily safer. Most new tasks build on established paradigms and share their general properties, such as right-skewed response time distributions. To threaten online research, an agent need not reproduce every effect, only produce plausibly human data.

A second limitation concerns the online sample. We could not verify whether its respondents were human. It also differed from the lab sample in how it was collected, on participants' own devices and in uncontrolled environments, so differences between the online and lab samples cannot be attributed to agents alone.

In addition, the SVMs learned what human data look like from students tested in the lab, not from online participants, so they may flag online participants simply for differing from this reference sample. A third limitation concerns the features. Our SVMs used eight summary features of response times and task accuracy, and finer-grained features based on theoretical predictions about the task, such as effects of individual stimulus properties, may separate agents from humans better. Finally, online sample providers and hosting platforms can also monitor other signals during data collection, such as mouse movements, keystroke timing, or browser information. Our study addressed the case in which such checks are not in place or are not sufficient, which still applies to most behavioral experiments.

Taken together, these results show that a human-like Stroop effect no longer implies a human participant. AI agents can produce behavioral data that pass conventional screening, and the false alarms of both SVMs and the failure of the supervised SVM to generalize to a second agent limit their usefulness for identifying agent participation in online samples. As agentic systems improve, protecting online behavioral research will depend less on inspecting data after collection and more on verifying who produced them.

Continued tests with independently developed agents and verified online samples are needed to establish which safeguards can meet that challenge.

Evaluation Scheme

Table S2 reports the means next to the medians of the 5,000 Monte Carlo splits, and the results of two evaluation schemes that use more data for training, repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation and leave-one-out cross-validation. Across these schemes, the one-class SVM classified .63 to .67 of the test respondents correctly and the supervised SVM .93 to .94; the supervised SVM wrongly flagged .10 to .12 of the lab test respondents.

With more training data, the one-class SVM flagged fewer lab test respondents (specificity .57 to .59 instead of .38).

Separation by Individual Features

The SVMs combined eight features. To show which features separated the lab and AEA samples on their own, we computed the mean and standard deviation of each feature in each sample and its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC;

Table S3) across all 51 lab and 51 AEA respondents, without a classifier. The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen AEA respondent and a randomly chosen lab respondent are ordered correctly by the feature, in whichever direction separated the samples better; .50 means no separation and 1.00 perfect separation.

Stricter Decision Thresholds and Class Weights

When agents are rare, most flags of the supervised SVM would be false alarms (Table 4 in the main text). We therefore tested whether more cautious settings, that is, a stricter decision threshold (a higher cut-off on the SVM's score, so the SVM needs more evidence before flagging a respondent) or class weights matching a lower contamination rate, would reduce false alarms without missing more AEA respondents (Table S4). Each threshold was set on the training data of a split, at the 95th or 99th percentile of the cross-validated scores of the 25 lab training respondents. Because each setting changes the sensitivity and specificity, these were measured again on the held-out respondents of the same 5,000 splits. Class weights were set proportional to the assumed contamination rate; the main analysis used equal weights.

On average, stricter thresholds and class weights for a lower contamination rate reduced false alarms only by missing more AEA respondents, and no setting combined high sensitivity with a high positive predictive value at 5% contamination.
