Generalization to a Second Agent

A supervised SVM is useful only if it also detects respondents from an agent it was not trained on. We therefore tested the supervised SVM on data from a second agent.

Supplemental Material

This supplement reports four additional analyses of the two support vector machines (SVMs) described in the main text and a completed REFORMS checklist. The analyses test whether the results depend on the analysis choices, show which features separated the lab and artificial experiment agent (AEA) samples, test more cautious settings of the supervised SVM, and test whether the supervised SVM detects a second agent.

Robustness of Analysis Choices

Several analysis choices were fixed in advance: the setting ν of the one-class SVM and the evaluation by 5,000 random splits into training and test sets. To test whether the results depended on these choices, we varied ν and compared the main evaluation with schemes that use more data for training.

Setting of the One-Class SVM

Table S1 shows the performance of the one-class SVM for values of ν from .01 to .50. The median classifier accuracy stayed between .62 and .63 for all values, and sensitivity and specificity were the same for all values up to .30.

Method

We collected data from 51 respondents generated by a second agent, the artificial general experiment agent (AGEA), in October 2026. The AGEA was developed by the first author as part of a separate research project (Özüdoğru, Chetverikov, et al., 2026) and was designed to complete behavioral experiments in general rather than the Stroop task alone.

The AGEA completed the same task, and its data were processed and analyzed with the same methods as the lab and AEA data. In each of the same 5,000 splits, one supervised SVM was trained on lab and AEA respondents and another on lab and AGEA respondents (25 of each), and both were tested on held-out lab, AEA, and AGEA respondents (26 of each).

Results

Each SVM detected the agent it was trained on but missed most respondents of the other agent (Table S5). The SVM trained on AEA data flagged 19% of the AGEA respondents, and the SVM trained on AGEA data flagged 35% of the AEA respondents.

Balanced accuracy fell from .94 to .54 and from .96 to .67, respectively. It fell in every split, except for one split in which the two balanced accuracies of the SVM trained on AGEA data were tied. Both SVMs still gave the other agent's respondents higher scores than lab respondents, but most of these scores stayed below the default decision threshold.

We did not test whether another threshold, chosen without data from the other agent, would detect it.

Figure 1The Color-Word Stroop Task

Features.

We identified eight data properties that a researcher can compute from our trial data. These eight features were used as the input variables for both SVMs. Mean response time and the standard deviation of response times describe how fast and how variable response times are. Skewness of response times was included because human response time distributions have a long tail of slow responses(Heathcote et al., 1991), and a lack of this skew has been discussed as a sign of agent data(Huskey et al., 2026; Van der Stigchel et al., 2026). Task accuracy, the proportion of correct responses, indicates whether the task was done as instructed. Response time drift, the slope of response time across trials, was included because humans speed up with practice or slow down with fatigue during a task, whereas an agent need not. Lag-one autocorrelation of response times was included because the response times of successive human trials are correlated(Laming, 1979), and this correlation has also been discussed as a sign of agent data(Huskey et al., 2026; Van der Stigchel et al., 2026). Finally, interference (incongruent minus neutral) and facilitation (neutral minus congruent) in mean correct response time are the two components ofthe Stroop effect (MacLeod, 1991). The response time features used all trials with a response, so lag-one autocorrelation was computed between successive responses, including pairs separated by a missed trial or a break; task accuracy was based on all 288 trials. The first six features can be computed for any response time task; interference and facilitation require the Stroop conditions. We used one feature per property, because several candidate features overlapped or were derived from each other.
